name: Papaya enzyme hair inhibitor

card.summary: Folk idea that papaya's papain enzyme slows hair regrowth; the enzyme is real, the hair claim has no published trials behind it.
card.aka: Papain hair inhibitor, papaya hair-growth retardant
card.note: The FDA acted against unapproved topical papain drug products in 2008 after allergic reaction reports; latex allergy may raise risk.

quick.overview:
Papain is a protein-digesting enzyme from papaya, used in meat tenderisers, wound debridement and some cosmetics. A folk and cosmetic-marketing idea holds that applying papaya or papain can weaken hair or slow regrowth after removal.

No published study located tested this claim.
quick.mechanism: Papain is a cysteine protease that breaks down proteins. Proponents reason that it could degrade hair protein or follicle structures; this has not been tested in published human studies.
quick.risks: In 2008 the US FDA moved against marketing of unapproved topical papain drug products, citing reports of allergic reactions causing low blood pressure and rapid heart rate. People with latex allergy may be at higher risk of reacting to topical papain.

lead: Papain, also called papaya proteinase I, is a cysteine protease enzyme found in papaya (Carica papaya). It has commercial uses in leather, cosmetics, textiles, detergents, food and pharmaceuticals, is the active ingredient in many meat tenderisers, and appears in enzymatic wound-debriding products.[1]

The idea that papaya enzyme inhibits hair growth circulates as a folk and cosmetic claim. The reference text for papain makes no hair-related claims, and no clinical studies were found on it for this purpose.[1]

paras: Papain is the namesake of the papain-like protease family. Beyond food and cosmetics, it is used to dissociate tissue in cell-culture work and in a gel for removing tooth decay.[1] Pre-contact South American peoples are recorded as using papaya to tenderise meat.[1]

In 2008 the US FDA moved to stop marketing of topical papain drug products sold without approval, citing reports of allergic reactions with low blood pressure and rapid heart rate. Because papain comes from papaya, people with latex allergy may be at higher risk of reacting.[1]

timeline.event: US FDA moves to stop marketing of unapproved topical papain drug products after allergic reaction reports.[1]
